summary:
What did we develop?
We developed ORBITAL, an interactive space mission design and simulation game built in Unity with an embedded web-based interface. Players design custom spacecraft and launch vehicles, manage critical resources (delta-v, mass, power, and thermal budgets), execute orbital maneuvers, and conduct scientific observation campaigns across Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

How does it address the challenge?
Addressing the Space Mission Design Game challenge, ORBITAL bridges complex orbital mechanics and mission planning with engaging, interactive gameplay. It integrates real NASA datasets—including MODIS flood/wildfire observations and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA/Diviner) topography and thermal data—transforming real-world mission planning trade-offs and scientific downlinks into playable learning mechanics.

Why is it important?
Aerospace concepts and Earth observation data can be daunting to the public. ORBITAL demystifies space exploration by allowing learners to test engineering constraints, experience real planetary science workflows, and discover how satellite data directly benefits planetary monitoring and space exploration.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

ORBITAL is an educational space systems engineering and orbital mission simulation game designed as a hybrid desktop application combining a Unity 3D physics simulation with an embedded mission control workstation. Players act as spacecraft architects and flight directors across a 28-mission campaign covering Earth observation, lunar landings, planetary exploration, and deep-space trajectories. In the workshop, players build modular satellites and multi-stage launch vehicles, balancing payload mass, power generation, battery storage, thermal management (radiators and insulation), attitude control, and radio antennas. Once launched, players execute orbital maneuvers and manage real-time spacecraft operations—such as eclipse battery drains, component temperature limits, antenna alignment, recorder capacity, and communication delays—to collect and downlink scientific observations before mission deadlines.

2. What benefits does it have?

ORBITAL teaches authentic aerospace engineering and scientific data literacy through hands-on gameplay. Rather than using simplified arcade mechanics, it forces players to confront real-world engineering trade-offs, such as how adding a larger sensor increases mass, power consumption, and thermal buildup, which in turn demands a heavier propulsion system and larger rocket. It features pre-flight test fixtures (such as eclipse and ground-station pass simulations) so players can validate their designs before launch. Additionally, it operates entirely offline with bundled historical space data, making it completely accessible in classrooms and low-connectivity environments without requiring online accounts or external servers.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project is built to make aerospace engineering and planetary science engaging and accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts, including participants in events like the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. By aligning with NASA Systems Engineering principles, it bridges textbook physics and practical mission design. It also promotes scientific integrity by requiring players to critically assess returned data—teaching them that raw measurements carry uncertainties, such as distinguishing an active fire hotspot from total burned area or recognizing that cold lunar surface temperatures do not automatically confirm the presence of water ice.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Game Engine & Host: Unity 6 (version 6000.6.8f1) using the Built-in Render Pipeline (Windows x64, Direct3D 11).
    • C# (.NET Framework): Core numerical simulation, orbital physics, launcher executable, and native bridge between Unity and the embedded browser runtime.
    • JavaScript / Node.js (ES6+): Mission control workstation interface, campaign progression, scenario debriefs, and automated asset-packaging pipelines.
    • Python: Offline data processing pipelines, mathematical verification scripts, and asset restoration utilities.
    • HTML5 & Modern CSS: High-density, responsive Mission Control telemetry consoles and instrument displays.
  • Runtimes & Frameworks: Microsoft WebView2 Evergreen for embedding the browser-based mission control UI inside the native Unity window.
  • Hardware Requirements: Runs on standard Windows 10/11 x64 consumer laptops or desktops (both integrated and discrete GPUs, minimum display resolution of 1280×720).

5. How is your project creative?

ORBITAL uniquely bridges real-time 3D orbital mechanics with a dense, interactive mission operations dashboard that mirrors the look and feel of a real space agency flight console. It creatively incorporates real historical NASA mission datasets directly into playable objectives, including NASA LANCE/MODIS flood maps, NASA FIRMS active fire detections, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA/Diviner) polar elevation and temperature data, and Kepler space telescope exoplanet transit light curves. Furthermore, missions conclude with a realistic three-pillar debrief evaluating whether the spacecraft physically survived, whether critical data was downlinked in time, and what conclusions the returned evidence actually supports.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team focused heavily on balancing realistic physical modeling with intuitive gameplay, ensuring that astrodynamic concepts remain accessible to beginners without oversimplifying the engineering constraints. We prioritized low-spec classroom accessibility, testing the software to run offline on standard school laptops at 1280×720 resolution with full keyboard navigation and high-contrast visuals. We also emphasized software reliability and build determinism by creating an automated packaging pipeline with SHA-256 cryptographic hashes for asset integrity. Finally, we maintained strict adherence to open-source licensing and scientific provenance, using authentic public-domain NASA datasets with transparent source documentation while replacing ambiguous third-party 3D assets with clean procedural models.

7. Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Explanation / Disclosure: Super Intelligence (Large Language Models / AI coding assistants) was used to accelerate development and support technical implementation. Specifically:
  • Code and Data: SI tools assisted in drafting, refactoring, and debugging C# Unity scripts, JavaScript UI bridge logic, and Python numerical validation tools. SI usage is acknowledged in the codebase documentation and file metadata. No NASA logos, insignias, or restricted design marks were generated or altered.
  • Text and Documentation: AI tools assisted in organizing mission debrief text, technical readouts, and engineering guidance templates.
  • Images, Audio, and Video: No SI-generated deepfakes, voices, or synthetic media were used; all graphics use native Unity rendering, procedural shaders, and verified public domain NASA data assets.
  • 3d models: some of the 3d models were genrated by ai including the rocket models
